text: Inanna Returns: Why Someone Else Must Stay Behind
Before Inanna entered the underworld, she had already arranged a way to call for help.
She told her attendant Ninshubur:
If I do not return, go to the gods for help.
Then she came to the first gate of the underworld.
The gatekeeper asked why she had come and carried word to Ereshkigal, queen of the underworld.
Inanna had to pass through seven gates.
At each one, an item of dress or an emblem of power was taken from her. Crown, beads, breast ornament, scepter, and clothing left her body one by one.
She asked why.
The answer was:
These are the rules of the underworld. Do not question them.
At last she stood naked before the gods of the underworld. She was judged and killed, and her corpse was hung up.
Ninshubur sought help as agreed.
Enki fashioned two tiny beings and sent them into the underworld to respond to Ereshkigal's suffering, obtain Inanna's corpse, and restore her to her feet with the substances of life.
The story seems to have reached resurrection.
But Inanna has not yet truly returned.
The underworld does not let anyone leave unconditionally.
To get out, she must provide someone else in her place.
And so demons follow Inanna back to the world above, searching for the one who must stay behind.
Resurrection is not the end of the story.
It merely changes the question from “How can she be rescued?” to “Who will pay for her return?”
Inanna has reason to leave the underworld.
She has died, and she has been rescued.
It is easy to take her side, to wish the gate would open at once and let her return to her former place.
But the underworld in this story has its own law:
Anyone who leaves must leave a substitute behind.
The story does not first establish for us whether this law is just.
It simply appears as a condition that cannot be bypassed.
This is precisely the form in which many unjust institutions are strongest.
They do not necessarily demand that you acknowledge their rules as right.
They demand only that, when you want to leave, you still choose from the options those rules provide.
Remain there yourself.
Or make someone else stay.
When every exit places the loss on somebody, a choice does not become free and innocent just because “it is up to you.”
The demons first encounter Ninshubur.
She is dressed in mourning, grieving for Inanna.
Inanna refuses to hand her over.
They then encounter two others who are also in mourning, and she spares them too.
Finally, she sees Dumuzi.
In the surviving account, he is splendidly dressed, sitting in a prominent place, and not mourning in the way she expects.
Inanna fixes her gaze on him and hands him over to the demons.
This detail is often used to arrive at a swift verdict of justice:
The others grieved for her, so they deserve to be spared.
Dumuzi did not grieve, so he ought to go to the underworld in her place.
But there is still a long way between “not mourning” and “deserving to die in someone else's place.”
Dumuzi's attitude may change how Inanna understands their relationship.
It may give her reason for anger, disappointment, even ending the relationship.
Yet that alone cannot automatically make him an equivalent substitute for her.
The story has not resolved the question of proportion.
It has simply given someone newly returned from death the position from which to designate someone else to enter it.
After escaping harm, is a victim still responsible for the cost she passes on to someone else?
This is a difficult question to ask.
It can all too easily sound like blaming the victim:
If you cannot guarantee that no one will suffer, you should stay where you are.
Such a demand is plainly unjust.
Inanna has no duty to accept her death forever just because the underworld has made a rule requiring substitutes.
That does not make her search for rescue wrong.
Conversely, having been harmed does not automatically remove her responsibility for decisions she later makes about a third person.
Both things must be held together:
She should not be trapped there.
Nor should Dumuzi simply become someone available for use because she has to get out.
If we say only the first, her return hides a second person's disappearance behind a victory.
If we say only the second, we place the entire burden of creating a way out that harms no one on the captive.
What truly creates this dilemma is the rule of the underworld.
But when the rule places the choice before Inanna, she still becomes the one who must decide.
Being forced to choose is not the same as having no choice at all.
It may lessen, alter, or even redistribute responsibility, but it does not make the resulting consequences disappear from the world.
This is also why a “substitute” is crueler than an ordinary exchange.
Exchange usually assumes that both parties enter the same transaction, each knowing what they give and receive.
With substitution, however, one person often recovers their place while another enters a loss they had no part in creating.
The original order appears to remain in balance:
The underworld is not one person short.
But this balance counts only numbers.
It does not ask who stays, whether they consent, or whether two people's lives can replace one another.
In the institution's eyes, one place goes out and another comes in. The books balance.
In people's lives, however, there are no two lives that are wholly interchangeable.
Inanna's return does not make Dumuzi's departure merely the other side of the same event.
For Inanna, it is restoration.
For Dumuzi, it is loss.
“An unchanged total” cannot settle these two opposite movements into a neutral result.
The surviving text itself also warns us not to read the story too neatly.

Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld is not a single tablet preserved intact from beginning to end, but a composite text assembled from many fragments. Scholars have also proposed that Inanna's rescue and Dumuzi's capture may originally have belonged to different traditions, joined later into their present form.
This does not make the story meaningless.
On the contrary, it urges caution:
We cannot explain every action as part of a psychological process that one character planned in full from the outset.
Inanna's reasons for descending, the meaning of the seven gates, and why Dumuzi occupies that position should not be too readily recast as a modern fable of personal growth.
Above all, we should not call each ornament taken from her “letting go of a self,” as though, after losing all power and clothing, a person finally discovers their true inner being.
The text describes dispossession, death, rescue, and substitution.
These things are already weighty enough in themselves.
There is no need to turn them into steps in a spiritual upgrade.
At the seven gates, Inanna keeps asking:
Why?
Each time, the gatekeeper answers with the rules.
Here, the rules do not explain themselves.
They merely demand acceptance from whoever passes through.
When she wants to leave, the same structure appears again:
These are the customs of the underworld.
Someone must stay behind.
Where can an institution most easily hide responsibility?
Inside “That is how things have always been.”
When rules are presented as having no maker, no alternative, and no reason that needs explaining, everyone can only struggle against everyone else within them.
The conflict between Inanna and Dumuzi can obscure the real questions:
Why must one person's freedom depend on another person's captivity?
Why does the rescue system concern itself only with restoring the rescued person, without addressing the structure that must keep swallowing substitutes?
Why can everyone discuss only who deserves to stay, rather than whether anyone should have to stay at all?
The story offers no route to overturning the underworld's law.
This is exactly the pressure it puts on later readers.
We can see the injustice, but we cannot invent exits for the characters that did not exist for them then.
We can only refuse to mistake the absence of an exit for proof of justice.
Later, Dumuzi flees and is pursued, and Geshtinanna enters the tradition of taking turns to bear the burden.
How the different texts connect these stories is not altogether simple.
But this surviving composite narrative alone already contains an ending that cannot easily be smoothed over:
Inanna has returned.
And behind her returning footsteps come demons demanding a substitute.
This makes “rebirth” something more than a radiant word.
Some people's recovery really does depend on other people's labor, care, burdens, and yielding of their place.
That is not necessarily unjust in itself.
No one can always return to life entirely on their own.
But the more a recovery is supported by others, the less it can turn those supporters into a nameless cost.
Still less can “At last, I am back” automatically settle the whole account.
Someone's escape from harm is worth celebrating.
Those who helped them escape deserve to be seen.
And anyone pushed into another loss by that escape must not disappear from the story simply because they are not at the center of its picture of victory.
Inanna's return is not false.
She really does rise again, and she really does leave the underworld.
The problem is simply this:
Her return has not made death vanish into thin air.
It has changed whom death falls upon.
That prevents the story from closing with “Life has conquered death.”
Nor can we simply say that, because Inanna designated Dumuzi, she did not deserve rescue.
The harm she suffered and the consequences she later caused need not cancel each other out.
A person can have the right to escape injustice and still make decisions in escaping for which they must answer.
The world's hardest situations often do not contain only innocent people and perpetrators.
Rather, someone first harmed by a rule is later pushed by that same rule into deciding who will be harmed next.
Then acknowledging what she suffered cannot make a third person's cost disappear.
Nor should questioning that cost become a demand that she stay forever.
Inanna finally returns to the world above.
What has not been brought back is the possibility of letting her leave without handing someone else over.

*Textual basis: the modern composite text of the Sumerian Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld, focusing on the stripping at the seven gates, Inanna's death and rescue, the requirement to provide a substitute to leave the underworld, and the passages in which she first spares the mourners and finally hands Dumuzi over. The work is assembled from multiple cuneiform sources; the relationship between the formation of the rescue and capture sections remains a subject of scholarly debate. This essay does not blend it with the later Akkadian Descent of Ishtar, nor interpret the seven gates as a fixed sequence of modern psychological stages.*
